title: Client Density
summary: Hundreds of devices sharing the air in a crowded unit without slowing each other down.

opener.promise: Serve many devices at once, across several bands
opener.problem: At shift change, hundreds of devices compete for the same radio time.

wifi7Adds: Wi-Fi 6 introduced OFDMA {{ofdma-ax}} and BSS coloring {{bss-coloring-ax}} for crowded spaces; Wi-Fi 7 adds wider channels {{eht-max-width}} and multi-link load balancing {{mlo-bands}}.

beats.heading: Shift change in the emergency department

caption.headline: Shift change in the emergency department
caption.takeaway: Crowded units fail from too little [[airtime|airtime]] per device, not from weak signal.

beats.body:
At shift change, an emergency department fills with devices: two shifts of staff phones and [[voice-badge|badges]], bedside monitors, infusion pumps, workstations on wheels, plus patients' and visitors' phones.

With Wi-Fi 5 and earlier, devices sending to the access point take turns, one at a time {{contention-dcf}}; Wi-Fi 5 can send to a few devices at once only in the other direction {{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}. The more devices there are, the longer each one waits — and small, urgent messages wait just as long as large downloads.
beats.bottomLine: In crowded areas, Wi-Fi often fails from too many devices sharing too little airtime, not from weak signal.
beats.sceneDescription: Shift change, shown as hospital elevators. Devices queue in the lobby waiting to send, and each elevator trip stands for one transmission to the access point. With one sending device per trip, new devices join faster than the elevator can carry them, so the queue grows and the devices that have waited longest turn amber, then red.

callout.title: Why crowded units slow down
points: Sending devices take turns, one per transmission{{contention-dcf}}
At shift change, devices arrive faster than turns come round
Small urgent messages wait as long as big downloads

beats.heading: Every device shares the same airtime

caption.headline: Every device shares the same airtime
caption.takeaway: Plan capacity, not just coverage: peak device counts decide how a unit performs.

beats.body: An [[access-point|access point]]'s capacity is its [[airtime]] — the time its channel spends carrying traffic. Every connected device draws from the same pool. Client density is how many devices share that pool, and density is rising as more clinical equipment becomes wireless.
beats.bottomLine: Capacity planning, not just coverage planning, decides how a unit performs at its busiest moments.
beats.sceneDescription: The same elevator, labeled as the access point’s airtime: one elevator shared by every device in the unit. The queue keeps growing and turning red, because every device draws on the same trips.

callout.title: Capacity is airtime
points: Every device on an access point shares its airtime
More devices means a longer wait for each one
Plan for peak device counts, not floor area

beats.heading: Serve many devices in each transmission

caption.headline: Serve many devices in each transmission
caption.takeaway: [[ofdma|OFDMA]], new in Wi-Fi 6, splits each transmission so several devices share it{{ofdma-ax}}.
caption.technical: Wi-Fi 5 sends to several devices only downlink{{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}; Wi-Fi 6 also lets several devices send at once{{he-ul-mu}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 5 already let an access point send to up to four devices at once with downlink MU-MIMO {{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}, but devices sending to it still took turns. Wi-Fi 6 introduced [[ofdma|OFDMA]], which splits each transmission into [[resource-unit|resource units]] so several devices are served at once, in both directions {{ofdma-ax}} {{he-ul-mu}}, and [[bss-coloring|BSS coloring]], which helps devices ignore distant neighboring networks {{bss-coloring-ax}}.

Wi-Fi 7 builds on both. Wider channels hold more resource units {{eht-max-width}}, and [[mlo|multi-link operation]] gives devices links in several bands {{mlo-bands}}.
beats.bottomLine: The same access point can serve more devices with less waiting, which is how dense units stay responsive.
beats.deepDive: Outside multi-user transmissions, the [[contention]]-based access defined in 802.11 lets one station use the whole channel per transmission opportunity {{contention-dcf}}. 802.11ac added downlink MU-MIMO to up to four stations {{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}. OFDMA assigns RUs to multiple stations in one [[ppdu|PPDU]], and 802.11ax adds triggered multi-user transmission from stations to the AP {{ofdma-ax}} {{he-ul-mu}}. BSS coloring lets a station treat inter-BSS frames differently for spatial reuse {{bss-coloring-ax}}. Wi-Fi 7 adds multi-link traffic steering per link {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. These are efficiency tools; which traffic goes first still depends on QoS classification.
beats.sceneDescription: The elevator now carries several sending devices on every trip, one per seat, labeled OFDMA, introduced with Wi-Fi 6: each seat stands for a resource unit, a slice of the transmission given to one device. The queue in the lobby shrinks trip by trip and the red devices clear.

questions.q: Do older devices benefit from OFDMA?
questions.a: No. Devices from before Wi-Fi 6 still take turns using the whole channel when they send{{contention-dcf}}. They benefit indirectly when newer devices finish sooner, but the full gains arrive as devices are refreshed.

questions.q: What does BSS coloring do on a dense floor?
questions.a: It tags each network’s transmissions so a device can tell its own network from a neighbor’s{{bss-coloring-ax}}, and reuse the channel more often instead of deferring to distant traffic.

questions.q: Didn’t Wi-Fi 5 already serve several devices at once?
questions.a: Yes, in one direction: downlink MU-MIMO lets a Wi-Fi 5 access point send to up to four devices together{{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}. Devices sending to the access point still took turns until Wi-Fi 6 let several send at once with OFDMA{{he-ul-mu}}{{ofdma-ax}}.

callout.title: What OFDMA does
points: Splits one transmission into slices called resource units
Each device gets its own slice, so several are served per trip
The queue clears instead of growing

beats.heading: One at a time, several at once, across bands

caption.headline: Taking turns, then sharing each trip
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 6 shares each trip both ways{{ofdma-ax}}; Wi-Fi 7 adds links in up to three bands{{mlo-bands}}.
caption.technical: Wi-Fi 5 shares only downlink trips{{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}. Older clients still contend for the channel{{contention-dcf}}.

beats.body:
For devices sending to the access point, Wi-Fi 5 serves one per transmission {{contention-dcf}}; it can send to a few at once only downlink {{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}. Wi-Fi 6 serves several at once in both directions {{ofdma-ax}} {{he-ul-mu}}.

Wi-Fi 7 keeps that and adds two things. With [[mlo|multi-link operation]], one device can hold links in the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands under a single connection {{mlo-bands}} {{mlo-tid-mapping}}, so the access point can send its traffic on a band with room; how many links a device uses at once depends on its mode {{emlsr-what}}. And in 6 GHz its channels can be 320 MHz wide {{eht-max-width}}, so each transmission has room for more devices.
beats.bottomLine: Each generation serves more devices per unit of airtime; Wi-Fi 7 also lets crowded units use several bands for the same devices.
beats.deepDive: Gains depend on device support: OFDMA and multi-link benefits apply to clients that support Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 respectively. Older clients still use contention and full-channel transmissions {{contention-dcf}}, so mixed device fleets see partial gains until devices are refreshed.
beats.sceneDescription: Two lobbies side by side with the same crowd arriving to send. On the left, the earlier generation: one elevator, carrying one sending device per trip for Wi-Fi 5 or several for Wi-Fi 6. On the right, Wi-Fi 7: three elevators, one each for the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands, each carrying several devices, labeled links in up to three bands. The Wi-Fi 7 queue empties fastest.

callout.title: How each generation does it
points: Wi-Fi 5: senders one per trip; downlink can share{{vht-dl-mu-mimo}}
Wi-Fi 6: several devices per trip, both ways, with OFDMA{{ofdma-ax}}
Wi-Fi 7: links in up to three bands, use depends on mode{{mlo-bands}}
One connection across its bands{{mlo-tid-mapping}}; wider channels fit more{{eht-max-width}}

beats.heading: Staying responsive at the busiest moments

caption.headline: Staying responsive at the busiest moments
caption.takeaway: Size each unit for peak device counts; Wi-Fi 7 raises the ceiling, but placement still matters.

beats.body:
Shift changes, mass-casualty events and full waiting rooms are exactly when clinical communication matters most — and when device counts peak. Serving more devices per transmission helps alerts, calls and charting stay responsive when the unit is busiest.

Design for peak density: count devices per bed and per staff member, not just square feet.
beats.bottomLine: Plan wireless capacity around peak device counts in each unit; Wi-Fi 7 raises the ceiling, but placement and channel planning still matter.
beats.sceneDescription: The Wi-Fi 7 lobby at the busiest moment: the crowd keeps arriving, three elevators carry several devices each trip, and hardly anyone is waiting. Rates are illustrative.

questions.q: How many devices can one access point handle?
questions.a: There is no single number: it depends on the traffic mix, channel width and how many devices support OFDMA and multi-link. Count devices per bed and per staff member at peak, and size from a site survey.

callout.title: What to plan
points: Count devices per bed and per staff member at peak
Older devices still take turns when sending until refreshed{{contention-dcf}}
Placement and channel planning still matter

values.wifi5: Several when the AP sends (MU-MIMO); one when devices send
